concept.name: REST Resource Modeling

relationships.description: Connects REST Resource Modeling to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

concept.tagline: Designing stable noun-centric HTTP APIs with sub-resource workflows, `Idempotency-Key` retries, `ETag` concurrency, and RFC 9457 errors.
concept.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of REST resource modeling—from reifying verbs into sub-resources to `Idempotency-Key`, `If-Match`, cursor pagination, and RFC 9457 Problem Details.

spark.summary: REST resource modeling organizes an API around stable, addressable nouns (resources) manipulated through standard HTTP verbs, status codes, and concurrency/idempotency headers rather than RPC-style action verbs.
spark.keyTakeaway: Model state transitions and workflows as explicit sub-resources (like `/orders/{id}/cancellations`) with `Idempotency-Key` and `ETag` headers so clients get safe retries, caching, and predictable HTTP semantics.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** **REST resource modeling** treats an API as a navigable graph of **resources (nouns)** rather than RPC verbs.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Reified Sub-Resource Workflow (`POST /refunds` + `202` + `ETag`) (Mobile Client -> Orders REST API -> Postgres + Idem); REST `Idempotency-Key` Request Deduplication States (NEW KEY -> COMMITTED -> CONFLICT / 422).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Standardize mutation and pagination contracts across your entire API surface. A public payments API enforces `Idempotency-Key` (24h TTL, SHA-256 request-body hash check returning `422` on payload mismatch) in the same ACID transaction as domain writes.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore idempotent APIs, optimistic concurrency, and API gateways.

learningJourney.title: What is REST Resource Modeling
learningJourney.explanation:
**REST resource modeling** treats an API as a navigable graph of **resources (nouns)** rather than RPC verbs. Core entities use plural collection URIs (`/v1/orders`, `/v1/orders/{orderId}`), while workflows and state transitions are reified as sub-resources (e.g., `POST /v1/orders/{id}/cancellations` or `POST /v1/exports` returning `202 Accepted` + `Location: /v1/exports/{jobId}`).

Every endpoint honors HTTP semantics strictly: `GET` is safe/idempotent, `PUT`/`DELETE` are idempotent, and `POST` becomes safely retryable via `Idempotency-Key`.

sectionDiagram.title: Reified Sub-Resource Workflow (`POST /refunds` + `202` + `ETag`)
sectionDiagram.summary: Atomic Idempotency-Key storage + 202 Location polling turn flaky mobile retries into safe, deterministic workflows.

learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how REST Resource Modeling works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Clean Resource Modeling (Lost Updates & Retry Duplicates)
learningJourney.explanation: APIs that tunnel RPC verbs through `POST /doAction` or mutate state on `GET` lose HTTP caching, break link-prefetchers, and suffer from **Lost Updates** (two clients `PUT`/`PATCH` without `If-Match`) and **Duplicate Side Effects** (retrying `POST /orders` after a 504 gateway timeout). Standardized `ETag` + `If-Match` (`412`), `Idempotency-Key` + payload hash (`422` on mismatch), and RFC 9457 `application/problem+json` errors eliminate these classes of bugs.

ideas.title: Shallow Nesting (Max 2 Levels)
ideas.description: Use `/v1/projects/{id}/issues` for scoped listing/creation, but expose `/v1/issues/{issueId}` at top level so URLs don't break if items move.

ideas.title: Opaque UUIDv7 / ULIDs Over Sequential Integers
ideas.description: Sequential IDs (`1, 2, 3`) leak business volume and invite IDOR enumeration—use UUIDv7 or prefixed ULIDs (`ord_01J...`).

learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Clean Resource Modeling under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Where REST shines (and where gRPC or GraphQL fit better)
learningJourney.explanation: Use REST for public, partner, and cacheable HTTP APIs; choose gRPC for internal low-latency streaming or GraphQL for deeply nested UI graphs.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Public/Partner APIs & Mobile Clients
benefits: Universal HTTP/CDN caching (`ETag`/`304`), OpenAPI 3.1 tooling, and built-in retry/concurrency headers.
costs: Can require multiple round-trips for deeply nested object graphs unless paired with BFFs.

benefits: Use **gRPC** with Protobuf over HTTP/2 for compact binary framing and streaming.

comparison.choice: Avoid: Arbitrary Nested UI Graph Queries
benefits: Use **GraphQL** when diverse UI screens query unpredictable entity graphs in one round-trip.
costs: GraphQL sacrifices standard HTTP URL-level CDN caching.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: How Cursor Pagination, `If-Match` & RFC 9457 Errors are implemented
learningJourney.explanation: Enforce keyset/cursor pagination (`?limit=50&cursor=...`) with a capped max limit (200) instead of `OFFSET` (which drifts under concurrent inserts and degrades to $O(\text{offset})$ scans), and return RFC 9457 `application/problem+json` on errors.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```http
PATCH /v1/orders/ord_01J9Z8K HTTP/1.1
If-Match: "v42"
Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json

{"shipping_tier": "express"}
```

```json
// RFC 9457 application/problem+json on ETag mismatch (HTTP 412)
{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/precondition-failed",
  "title": "Resource version conflict",
  "status": 412,
  "detail": "Expected ETag v42, but current version is v43.",
  "instance": "/v1/orders/ord_01J9Z8K"
}
```
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: `PUT` vs. `PATCH` & Offset vs. Cursor Pagination
learningJourney.explanation: Standardize mutation and pagination contracts across your entire API surface.

benefits: Saves bandwidth and avoids forcing clients to echo read-only or unknown fields.
costs: Requires careful handling of explicit `null` vs. omitted fields.

benefits: Simple, naturally idempotent semantics when clients own the full representation.
costs: Breaks forward compatibility if the server adds new fields older clients omit.

benefits: $O(1)$ indexed seek performance and zero skipped/duplicated rows under concurrent inserts.
costs: Cannot jump directly to arbitrary page #47.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: Production example: Idempotency + ETag + Cursor Envelope
learningJourney.explanation: A public payments API enforces `Idempotency-Key` (24h TTL, SHA-256 request-body hash check returning `422` on payload mismatch) in the same ACID transaction as domain writes, returns `ETag` on all `GET`s, and emits `Retry-After` on `429`.

sectionDiagram.summary: Hashing the canonical request body prevents a client from accidentally reusing an old Idempotency-Key for a new payload.

supportingConcepts.title: Problem: Idempotent APIs & Preventing Duplicate Charges

learningJourney.purpose: Applied problems: connect these internals to concrete system design and debugging scenarios.

knowledgeCheck.question: A client sends `POST /v1/orders/ord_91f/refunds` with `Idempotency-Key: k1` and `amount_cents: 4500`, then later sends the exact same `Idempotency-Key: k1` with `amount_cents: 9000`. What should the server return?

options.text: HTTP `422 Unprocessable Content` (or `400`) rejecting the payload mismatch against the stored request hash
options.feedback: Correct: always hash the canonical request body with the `Idempotency-Key` and reject mismatched payloads instead of silently replaying the old response.
That violates idempotency and risks double-refunding.

options.text: Return `200 OK` with the $45 refund silently
options.feedback: Silently returning a $45 response for a $90 request hides a serious client bug.

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
